ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: While empirical studies with human participants are often constrained by a relatively small number of measurements, research on LLM ratings enables the implementation of a fully crossed design with many facets to study the factors driving output variability.
table.header: A Simulation-Based Workflow for Evaluating LLM Ratings

table.text: If human ratings from experts or participants are already available or are planned to be collected for some or all of the items, LLM simulations may aim at investigating the relative or absolute agreement of LLM ratings with benchmark ratings (e.g., Fang et al., 2026; Martínez et al., 2024).
table.formatted: If human ratings from experts or participants are already available or are planned to be collected for some or all of the items, LLM simulations may aim at investigating the relative or absolute agreement of LLM ratings with benchmark ratings (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Fang et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al., 2024)</ref>.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> While empirical studies with human participants are often constrained by a relatively small number of measurements, research on LLM ratings enables the implementation of a fully crossed design with many facets to study the factors driving output variability.

> If human ratings from experts or participants are already available or are planned to be collected for some or all of the items, LLM simulations may aim at investigating the relative or absolute agreement of LLM ratings with benchmark ratings (e.g., Fang et al., 2026; Martínez et al., 2024).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.95 ", Sentence = "Ollama's built-in defaults (https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/v0.12.9/api/types.go and https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/v0.12.9/envconfig/config.go) are: Ollama defaults: • num_ctx = 4096 (context length in tokens; set via the environment variable OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH, which we did not change) 512 (maximum number of prompt tokens processed per forward pass) Model defaults (departures from Ollama defaults as defined in the Modelfiles): • gpt-oss (20b): temperature = 1 • gemma3 (4b, 12b, 27b): temperature = 1, top-k = 64, top-p = 0.95 However, ellmer accesses Ollama through its OpenAI-compatible endpoint (/v1; see https://github.com/tidyverse/ellmer/blob/v0.4.0/R/provider-ollama.R, line 81)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. #### README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including 'README' in the name of your overview document.

#### Registration's Source Project Is Closed

1 OSF source project is closed. The files metacheck lists below were not read from it — they were retrieved from the OSF registration's own copy, which is separate from and unaffected by the project's access setting. Nothing is currently lost, but this is still worth fixing: a closed source project means the files only survive for as long as the registration's copy does, and anyone who follows the project link itself (rather than the registration) will find it inaccessible.

- **https://osf.io/t2kar** is closed; its files were retrieved from the OSF registration https://osf.io/8e6gf, https://osf.io/8e6gf/overview.

Consider making the source project openly available.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: Evaluating Ratings from Large Language Models: A Simulation-Based Workflow

text.text: The present manuscript version (October 30, 2026)  was posted as a preprint on PsyArXiv (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/xphm9_v2).
text.formatted: The present manuscript version (October 30, 2026)  was posted as a preprint on PsyArXiv (<ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/xphm9_v2">https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/xphm9_v2</ref>).

text.text: The work was presented at the 1st Symposium on Metascience for Methods Research (Zürich, Switzerland) and at the 54th meeting of the German Society for Psychology (DGPs Luxembourg).
Data and R scripts for the analyses are available on Zenodo https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23810473.
text.formatted: Data and R scripts for the analyses are available on Zenodo <ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23810473">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23810473</ref>.

text.text: We used Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026) and DeepL Write (DeepL, 2026) for grammar checking and linguistic revision and reviewed all proposed changes.
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in psychological research to analyze and generate verbal data and stimulus materials.

Examples include analyzing large quantities of qualitative data (e.g., Chew et al., 2023; Player et al., 2025; Rathje et al., 2024; Smirnov, 2025), automating item scale construction (e.g., Barends & de Vries, 2025; Fyffe et al., 2023; Hommel et al., 2022), generating ratings of words, expressions, and phrases regarding psychological constructs (e.g., Hommel, 2023; Martínez et al., 2024), or using LLMs to simulate and estimate human behavior and judgments (e.g., Loru et al., 2025; von der Heyde et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Examples include analyzing large quantities of qualitative data (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Chew et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Player et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Rathje et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Smirnov, 2025)</ref>, automating item scale construction (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Barends & de Vries, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Fyffe et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Hommel et al., 2022)</ref>, generating ratings of words, expressions, and phrases regarding psychological constructs (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Hommel, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al., 2024)</ref>, or using LLMs to simulate and estimate human behavior and judgments (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Loru et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">von der Heyde et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In light of the numerous potential applications, it has been argued that LLMs have the capacity to facilitate various steps in the research process and to advance cognitive science (Feuerriegel et al., 2025; Wulff & Mata, 2025a).
text.formatted: In light of the numerous potential applications, it has been argued that LLMs have the capacity to facilitate various steps in the research process and to advance cognitive science <ref type="bibr">(Feuerriegel et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Wulff & Mata, 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: The present paper focuses on the application of LLMs to analyze and rate text stimuli.

For example, Martínez et al. (2024) used GPT-4o to generate ratings of valence (i.e., the pleasantness of a stimulus) and arousal (i.e., the intensity of emotional activation a stimulus elicits; Warriner et al., 2013) for multi-word expressions such as "hit rock bottom," "fall in love," or "ice cream cone."
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al. (2024)</ref> used GPT-4o to generate ratings of valence (i.e., the pleasantness of a stimulus) and arousal (i.e., the intensity of emotional activation a stimulus elicits; <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Warriner et al., 2013)</ref> for multi-word expressions such as "hit rock bottom," "fall in love," or "ice cream cone."

text.text: A defining feature of such tasks is that they involve a corpus of text stimuli (e.g., words, questionnaire items, sentences, social media posts, vignettes, etc.).

The stimuli are assumed to differ with respect to relevant features and LLMs are used to rate the stimuli automatically with respect to psychological constructs (arousal, valence), linguistic properties (grammatical complexity, concreteness), or other quantitative or qualitative information (topic modeling, presence or absence of certain informational cues).
Researchers using LLMs for such tasks are necessarily faced with the question of how to evaluate the quality of the generated ratings.
LLMs offer many impressive capabilities but also come with notable limitations for research use.

Both small and large models are known to be susceptible to hallucinations (Huang et al., 2025; Reddy et al., 2024) and they may generate synthetic response behavior that does not resemble that of human participants (Argyle et al., 2025; Hullman et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Both small and large models are known to be susceptible to hallucinations <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Huang et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Reddy et al., 2024)</ref> and they may generate synthetic response behavior that does not resemble that of human participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Argyle et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Hullman et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, LLMs may fall short in performing even seemingly simple tasks such as word counting (Markowitz, 2024).
text.formatted: Furthermore, LLMs may fall short in performing even seemingly simple tasks such as word counting <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Markowitz, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Despite their capacity to emulate plausible human responses in specific tasks, LLMs frequently do not succeed in replicating the full spectrum of human behavior.
This limitation is exemplified by the substantial reduction in variability of responses observed in LLM outputs compared to humans (Abdurahman et al., 2024; Martínez et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This limitation is exemplified by the substantial reduction in variability of responses observed in LLM outputs compared to humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abdurahman et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such issues and shortcomings have the potential to result in errors when relying on LLM output for making statistical inferences and drawing substantive conclusions (Hullman et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Such issues and shortcomings have the potential to result in errors when relying on LLM output for making statistical inferences and drawing substantive conclusions <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Hullman et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, it is imperative not to interpret LLM output at face value, as it has the potential to be misleading or false.
Utilizing LLMs in research responsibly necessitates the implementation of rigorous quality control measures (e.g., Argyle et al., 2025; Knöchel et al., 2025; Nestler et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Utilizing LLMs in research responsibly necessitates the implementation of rigorous quality control measures (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Argyle et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Knöchel et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Nestler et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: When aiming to use LLMs for a particular scientific task, researchers are faced with a multitude of different models and approaches.
In light of the abundance of available LLMs, the selection of a particular setup often involves arbitrary choices, which introduces researcher degrees of freedom.

Models differ in important aspects such as number of parameters, architecture, hyperparameter settings, and how and with which text corpora they have been trained (Argyle et al., 2025; Hussain et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Models differ in important aspects such as number of parameters, architecture, hyperparameter settings, and how and with which text corpora they have been trained <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Argyle et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Hussain et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Emerging applications of LLMs often rely on a single, promising LLM (e.g., Barends and de Vries, 2025; von der Heyde et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Emerging applications of LLMs often rely on a single, promising LLM (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Barends and de Vries, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">von der Heyde et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The selection of a particular model might be based on preliminary pilot testing or practical considerations such as accessibility and ease of use.
Output quality can be increased by systematic, iterative testing and may benefit from advanced methods such as fine-tuning (for a tutorial, see Conde et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Output quality can be increased by systematic, iterative testing and may benefit from advanced methods such as fine-tuning (for a tutorial, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Conde et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Reliance on a single model does not necessarily constitute a problem if its performance has been validated for the task at hand.
For example, Martínez et al. (2024) used GPT-4o to obtain ratings of valence, arousal, and concreteness for thousands of single words and multi-word expressions.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al. (2024)</ref> used GPT-4o to obtain ratings of valence, arousal, and concreteness for thousands of single words and multi-word expressions.

text.text: To validate their approach, they showed that the LLM ratings correlated highly both with existing human norms and with newly collected human ratings that were not part of the LLM training data.
However, once LLM output is used to draw scientific conclusions, it is important to investigate whether the results are robust across different models.
This is especially relevant given that new model variants with potential benefits (e.g., higher accuracy, increased efficiency, or reduced energy consumption) are continuously being developed.
A related issue is that LLM outcomes usually vary even when providing the same prompt repeatedly due to stochasticity inherent in model architecture (Demszky et al., 2023; Knöchel et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A related issue is that LLM outcomes usually vary even when providing the same prompt repeatedly due to stochasticity inherent in model architecture <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Demszky et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Knöchel et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, computational demands might be too high to repeat the same prompt inputs multiple times to study variability and to attain stable estimates.
As a remedy, one may enforce deterministic output by setting the temperature hyperparameter to zero.

However, such an approach artificially ignores the uncertainty of the underlying, stochastic model as it merely picks the most likely response option irrespective of whether it is clearly or only slightly preferred to the second-best option (Abdurahman et al., 2024; Martínez et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, such an approach artificially ignores the uncertainty of the underlying, stochastic model as it merely picks the most likely response option irrespective of whether it is clearly or only slightly preferred to the second-best option <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abdurahman et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Even if temperature is set to zero, this does still not guarantee deterministic output for some LLMs (Abdurahman et al., 2025).

text.text: Research investigating this problem often identified settings of other parameters, such as the batch size, as the cause for issues with reproducibility (Coqueret et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2025).

text.text: Furthermore, minor variations in prompt design may result in divergent outputs, thereby casting doubt on the validity, robustness, and generalizability of LLM output (e.g., Baumann et al., 2025; Cummins, 2026; Feuerriegel et al., 2026; Sclar et al., 2024).

text.text: Researchers have also criticized the usage of commercial LLMs since it is contingent upon proprietary services that may not be available to all researchers equally and do not adhere to open science principles (Balluff et al., 2026; Conde et al., 2026; Guest & van Rooij, 2025; Hussain et al., 2024).

text.text: As a remedy, researchers can use locally running, open LLMs for which the underlying model architecture and the parameter weights are known and available (Hussain et al., 2024), e.g., by using Ollama (Ollama, 2026).

text.text: The overview of limitations above shows that results obtained with one particular (commercial) LLM may not be robust to modifications of model and prompt parameters.

In line with good scientific practice, we recommend that researchers use open-weight LLMs and report the employed procedures and results transparently to ensure reproducibility and replicability of the research process (Abdurahman et al., 2025; Feuerriegel et al., 2025; Hussain et al., 2024; Knöchel et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In line with good scientific practice, we recommend that researchers use open-weight LLMs and report the employed procedures and results transparently to ensure reproducibility and replicability of the research process <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abdurahman et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Feuerriegel et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Hussain et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Knöchel et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: More importantly, it is essential to study the robustness and generalizability of LLM output across the multiverse of possible decisions regarding model choice, configuration, and prompt design (Hussain et al., 2024; Steegen et al., 2016).

text.text: Our evaluation framework thereby complements workflows focusing on method development via iterative improvement of LLM ratings (Conde et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Our evaluation framework thereby complements workflows focusing on method development via iterative improvement of LLM ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Conde et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Generalizability theory (Cronbach, 1972) provides a natural framework for analyzing ratings of different raters (e.g., LLM specifications) for a set of items (e.g., text stimuli) by partitioning the observed variance into systematic and error components.
text.formatted: Generalizability theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Cronbach, 1972)</ref> provides a natural framework for analyzing ratings of different raters (e.g., LLM specifications) for a set of items (e.g., text stimuli) by partitioning the observed variance into systematic and error components.

text.text: By distinguishing different sources of measurement error (termed facets), generalizability theory enables researchers to quantify the contributions of different factors.
Besides reducing unexplained variability, this provides a better understanding whether measurements generalize across different raters, items, and/or contexts (Brennan, 2001).
text.formatted: Besides reducing unexplained variability, this provides a better understanding whether measurements generalize across different raters, items, and/or contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brennan, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Generalizability theory and variance-decomposition approaches have recently been applied for specific LLM tasks, such as automated essay scoring (Song et al., 2026) and user intent extraction (Kunievsky & Evans, 2026), as well as for AI benchmarks (Hardy et al., 2026) , and have been advocated more generally for establishing the reliability of AI-based scores (Speer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Generalizability theory and variance-decomposition approaches have recently been applied for specific LLM tasks, such as automated essay scoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Song et al., 2026)</ref> and user intent extraction <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Kunievsky & Evans, 2026)</ref>, as well as for AI benchmarks <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Hardy et al., 2026)</ref> , and have been advocated more generally for establishing the reliability of AI-based scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Speer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Generalizability theory is particularly well-suited for studying the quality of LLM ratings in simulation studies, where output variability arises from multiple sources (e.g., prompt structure, model architecture, or stochasticity of the generation process).

While empirical studies with human participants are often constrained by a relatively small number of measurements, research on LLM ratings enables the implementation of a fully crossed design with many facets to study the factors driving output variability.
In a simulation, different models can be asked to rate all items in each combination of various conditions.
Across repeated prompts, LLMs can be called in a fresh context-free of prior conversation history-to ensure stochastic independence between measurements and conditions.
This high degree of methodological control enables a principled psychometric evaluation of LLM rating quality using generalizability theory.

From a pragmatic perspective, we recommend that researchers in psychology routinely employ a simulation-based workflow to evaluate the robustness of LLM-generated ratings for stimulus materials (e.g., words, sentences, test items, or vignettes), especially when there is no or little prior information regarding robustness of performance under different model and prompt parameters.
When systematically varying model and prompt specifications in a factorial design, researchers can apply principles established for simulation studies in methodological research.

Specifically, we adopt the ADEMP framework, which guides researchers in specifying the Aims, Data-generating mechanism, Estimands and targets, Methods, and Performance measures of a simulation study (Morris et al., 2019).

text.text: We modified the ADEMP-PreReg template (Siepe et al., 2024), which provides a systematic structure for planning, analyzing, and reporting simulation studies that evaluate the performance of different statistical methods (Siepe et al., 2024).

text.text: The template can also be used for preregistration, although the benefits and limitations of preregistering simulation studies remain debated (Siepe et al., 2026).

text.text: In the following, we develop a systematic simulation workflow to enable robust and transparent evaluation of LLM-generated ratings.
We adopt generalizability theory and propose concrete procedural steps for evaluating the quality of LLM ratings of verbal materials.

The modified ADEMP template for LLM simulation studies focuses on establishing a universally applicable, systematic workflow that can be utilized across diverse domains of psychological and social science research.
We will refer to this type of evaluation study as LLM simulation.

Note that other studies have employed similar terms (e.g., "LLM social simulations"; Anthis et al., 2025) to refer to research in which LLMs are employed to emulate hypothetical responses of human participants (so called "silicon samples", Cummins, 2026).
text.formatted: Note that other studies have employed similar terms (e.g., "LLM social simulations"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Anthis et al., 2025)</ref> to refer to research in which LLMs are employed to emulate hypothetical responses of human participants (so called "silicon samples", <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Cummins, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, our use of the term LLM simulation refers to the systematic evaluation and variation of methodological design choices when eliciting LLM ratings.
A complementary line of work has proposed prompting guidelines for various research purposes (e.g., Conde et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Giray, 2023; Ziems et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A complementary line of work has proposed prompting guidelines for various research purposes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Conde et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Fang et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Giray, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Ziems et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For example, prompts should be clear, precise and contain definitions of the target constructs.

Furthermore, prompt instructions may be accompanied by example cases illustrating the task, which is referred to as few-shot prompting, and prompts may assign roles to the LLM (e.g., "You are a statistics expert," Conde et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Furthermore, prompt instructions may be accompanied by example cases illustrating the task, which is referred to as few-shot prompting, and prompts may assign roles to the LLM (e.g., "You are a statistics expert," <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Conde et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Fang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, none of these prompting approaches is a safeguard against perturbations in the prompts, as studies have repeatedly found that subtle changes in prompts can elicit major variations in LLM responses (Alahmari et al., 2025; Sclar et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, none of these prompting approaches is a safeguard against perturbations in the prompts, as studies have repeatedly found that subtle changes in prompts can elicit major variations in LLM responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alahmari et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Sclar et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, specific recommendations are necessarily limited in scope, since they may not transfer across research domains and tasks, across models, or across time, given the rapid development of new models.
In contrast, our proposed framework and template are sufficiently general to evaluate a wide range of LLM pipelines for diverse research questions.
The two approaches complement each other.

While prompting guidelines suggest promising prompt designs, our evaluation workflow allows researchers to test whether these designs actually improve the quality of LLM ratings in a given application by including them as method factors.
In methodological simulation studies, researchers typically define a data-generating mechanism to simulate a large number of synthetic datasets.
Next, different statistical methods are applied to each dataset.
The employed methods are then evaluated using different performance measures that reflect how well each method achieves its goal (Morris et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The employed methods are then evaluated using different performance measures that reflect how well each method achieves its goal <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Morris et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Using this approach, researchers aim to draw conclusions regarding properties of different methods and make recommendations for applied data analysis under a specified set of conditions (Siepe et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Using this approach, researchers aim to draw conclusions regarding properties of different methods and make recommendations for applied data analysis under a specified set of conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Siepe et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It is useful to adopt this general approach to study the multiverse of possibilities in LLM prompting.
An LLM simulation study is characterized by systematically varying procedural details when generating ratings using different model specifications and prompt structures.
The quality of the resulting item ratings is then evaluated using one or more performance measures.
This allows researchers to quantify which design choices are critical for obtaining LLM-generated ratings in a specific application scenario.

For example, researchers can quantify the consistency between various LLMs' ratings or assess whether the inter-rater reliability with human ratings depends on specific aspects of the prompting procedure.
Despite many similarities, simulation studies evaluating statistical methods also differ from those evaluating LLM-generated ratings in important ways.
In LLM simulations, it is particularly important to distinguish three types of variability that affect the obtained output.
First, the variance of LLM ratings depends on the latent variability in the rated feature dimension across items.
This type of variance constitutes construct variance, which is the target of generated ratings.
To ensure a sufficient amount of construct variance, the items to be rated should be a representative sample from the target domain of interest.
The definition of the target domain determines the generalizability of the observed findings to other items from this domain that have not been studied (Brennan, 2001).
text.formatted: The definition of the target domain determines the generalizability of the observed findings to other items from this domain that have not been studied <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brennan, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Second, systematically varying prompts and models enables researchers to estimate method variance in observed LLM ratings.
1 Third, LLM ratings are inherently stochastic and can vary even when using the same model and prompt for the same item repeatedly.

This type of variability across iterations is particularly important for judging a model's degree of residual variance (i.e., stochastic error), which determines the stability of LLM responses to a particular task.
Note that low variability of LLM output to repeated, identical prompting does not imply that the provided response is correct.

Another important distinction between methodological simulation studies and LLM simulations concerns the data-generating mechanism.

When employing LLMs, the data-generation mechanism refers to the process of mapping the provided input (i.e., a specific prompt version providing instructions and the target item to be rated) to the output (e.g., ratings about psychological variables) by running a certain model configuration.
Many details of this process may be unknown or not clearly specified (e.g., the model architecture or parameter values).

Many state-of-the-art models have billions of parameters (e.g., between four and 70 billion parameters for typical open source models), which interact in complex ways, making it particularly difficult to understand the inner processing of LLMs (Feuerriegel et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Many state-of-the-art models have billions of parameters (e.g., between four and 70 billion parameters for typical open source models), which interact in complex ways, making it particularly difficult to understand the inner processing of LLMs <ref type="bibr">(Feuerriegel et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to statistical simulation studies, LLM simulations do not aim at recovering some known, "true" parameters of the (underspecified) data-generating model.
Instead, they aim at evaluating the quality of the obtained LLM output with respect to the task of interest (e.g., whether LLM ratings provide a sufficiently close approximation to a gold standard).

The modified ADEMP framework for LLM simulation studies, illustrated in Figure 1, addresses the specific requirements of evaluating LLM ratings of psychological constructs for text stimuli based on generalizability theory.

The Aims section describes the overarching goal of the LLM simulation study.
Researchers are typically interested in evaluating the ability of different LLMs to fulfill a particular rating task.

In initial research stages, however, human ratings may not be available, which calls for different strategies for the preliminary validation of the LLM output.
Depending on whether an external validation criterion is available, one can distinguish two aims.
The illustrated ADEMP workflow in Figure 1 highlights the distinction between assessing LLM ratings in terms of consistency and in terms of agreement with a gold standard.
text.formatted: The illustrated ADEMP workflow in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref> highlights the distinction between assessing LLM ratings in terms of consistency and in terms of agreement with a gold standard.

text.text: Irrespective of whether human ratings are available as a benchmark, LLM simulations may aim at evaluating the robustness and consistency of ratings across various LLM specifications.
In psychometric terms, this reflects the amount of method variance in observed ratings due to asking multiple raters (i.e., different LLMs and prompt instructions).

Potential aims might include conducting a variance decomposition of LLM ratings regarding items, models, and prompting approaches, or assessing inter-rater reliability between different LLMs or between the stochastic, repeated output of the same LLM.
Variance decomposition offers the advantage of reducing the number of comparisons and eliminating the need to define one of the LLM variants as a benchmark for comparison.

The variance explained by method factors such as the employed model or prompt structure should account for only a relatively small proportion of the variance compared to the construct variance across items.
Such a variance decomposition allows researchers to assess whether variability-or, conversely, consistency-in LLM ratings is due to factors exogenous or endogenous to the model (Sundh et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Such a variance decomposition allows researchers to assess whether variability-or, conversely, consistency-in LLM ratings is due to factors exogenous or endogenous to the model <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Sundh et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: If human ratings from experts or participants are already available or are planned to be collected for some or all of the items, LLM simulations may aim at investigating the relative or absolute agreement of LLM ratings with benchmark ratings (e.g., Fang et al., 2026; Martínez et al., 2024).
text.formatted: If human ratings from experts or participants are already available or are planned to be collected for some or all of the items, LLM simulations may aim at investigating the relative or absolute agreement of LLM ratings with benchmark ratings (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Fang et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: If LLMs are used to extract information about an objective criterion (e.g., the factual truth of statements), the LLM simulation aims at assessing criterion validity, which can be estimated using measures of absolute agreement.

The aim of assessing how well LLMs map to a gold standard mirrors the goal of traditional simulation studies, in which a statistical method is evaluated with respect to its performance in recovering known, true parameters (Morris et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The aim of assessing how well LLMs map to a gold standard mirrors the goal of traditional simulation studies, in which a statistical method is evaluated with respect to its performance in recovering known, true parameters <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Morris et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: When using LLMs, the data-generating mechanism is the process of mapping the prompt input to observable output as generated by a certain model configuration.

However, the underlying process of how exactly the input is transformed, processed, and analyzed by an LLM is often unknown and difficult to grasp (Abdurahman et al., 2024), even if it can be formally specified with mathematical equations and parameter values.
text.formatted: However, the underlying process of how exactly the input is transformed, processed, and analyzed by an LLM is often unknown and difficult to grasp <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abdurahman et al., 2024)</ref>, even if it can be formally specified with mathematical equations and parameter values.

text.text: What can, however, be specified when generating LLM ratings are analytical decisions at a more abstract level: (a) the selection or sampling of stimulus materials from the target domain and (b) the procedures employed to obtain LLM ratings regarding psychological features of interest.

Whereas the former aspect is relevant for the generalizability to other, new items from the target domain, the latter matters for the robustness and generalizability across different LLM specifications.

Accordingly, the Data-Generating Mechanism section contains information both about the type and selection of stimulus materials rated by the LLMs, and about the exact procedures of how LLM ratings will be elicited.
The stimulus materials used for LLM prompting (i.e., the corpus) can include statements, questions, vignettes, or items from a personality inventory.
First, researchers must define the target domain of the psychological (or linguistic) construct they wish to investigate.
Second, they need to decide on how to sample or construct stimuli that are representative for this domain (Cronbach, 1972).
text.formatted: Second, they need to decide on how to sample or construct stimuli that are representative for this domain <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Cronbach, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: The definition of the corpus and the selection of items to be included directly shape the scope and generalizability of findings about LLM-extracted features.

If the corpus consists only of statements assessing a particular psychological construct, the results of the LLM performance evaluation are informative only for comparable materials for the same construct.
Ideally, one would draw a true random sample of items from a well-defined target domain (Brennan, 2001).
text.formatted: Ideally, one would draw a true random sample of items from a well-defined target domain <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brennan, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: While this is practically difficult or even impossible, researchers should ensure that the verbal materials cover a sufficiently broad and heterogeneous subspace of the target domain to increase the generalizability of conclusions.
What constitutes sufficiently diverse data as input depends on the research question.
Initial attempts at extracting features via LLM prompting will likely involve user-friendly, interactive chat interfaces.
However, to render the generation of LLM ratings systematic, efficient, and reproducible, it should proceed in an automated and standardized manner.
Accordingly, the Data-Generating Mechanism section should describe all procedural details that are identical across all simulation conditions.

This includes the general design and structure of the LLM prompt input, while specific components of the prompt that vary across conditions (e.g., whether and which examples are given) should be reported in the Methods section.

One should also specify relevant details of the software employed to obtain LLM ratings, for instance, whether a remote, commercial service, a locally hosted, open-weights model, or an interactive chat interface will be used.
To ensure independence between ratings, it is important to use a fresh context when eliciting LLM responses (Conde et al., 2026).
text.formatted: To ensure independence between ratings, it is important to use a fresh context when eliciting LLM responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Conde et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: It should be reported how the models are accessed (e.g., via an API, that is, an application programming interface), and whether and how a specific response format (e.g., a numeric Likert rating between 1 and 7) was ensured.

For instance, it is possible to include specific instructions in the prompt to adhere to a certain response format or to use software features ensuring that the LLM output has a specific format, such as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation).

Note that the choice for structured output against an open format itself constitutes a researcher degree of freedom and could be explicitly varied to assess to what extent LLM ratings depend on this methodological factor.

We generally recommend using structured output for increasing standardization and software optimized for handling such output (e.g., the type_object() function family in the ellmer package in R; Wickham et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We generally recommend using structured output for increasing standardization and software optimized for handling such output (e.g., the type_object() function family in the ellmer package in R; <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Wickham et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: To ensure replicability of model calls, one should set random seeds, though this may not be possible for all models (Abdurahman et al., 2025).
text.formatted: To ensure replicability of model calls, one should set random seeds, though this may not be possible for all models <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abdurahman et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Reproducibility of LLM output also depends on hyperparameters such as temperature, top-k, and top-p that shape the distribution from which tokens are drawn.
While top-k sampling uses only the k tokens with the highest probability, top-p sampling uses the smallest set of tokens with a cumulative probability of p (Coqueret et al., 2026).
text.formatted: While top-k sampling uses only the k tokens with the highest probability, top-p sampling uses the smallest set of tokens with a cumulative probability of p <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Coqueret et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: When prompting an LLM, even details such as the batch size can alter the obtained output.

Full reproducibility is attainable only if a local model is run with fixed model and software versions, a fixed seed (or a temperature of 0), a controlled batch size, and identical hardware-conditions that are difficult to achieve in practice.
Yet, it is important to minimize stochasticity where possible, because reproducibility in LLMs is not all-or-nothing.
Fixing the seed, temperature and sampling parameters reduces unwanted variation and makes results more comparable.
This is especially valuable when repeating prompts many times is computationally prohibitive (Coqueret et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This is especially valuable when repeating prompts many times is computationally prohibitive <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Coqueret et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Yuan et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The Estimands and Targets section describes the purpose of the ratings to be generated by clarifying the theoretical construct(s) being studied.

In traditional, methodological simulation studies (Morris et al., 2019), the targets of interest are usually the unknown parameters of the data-generating mechanism, which are estimated with a statistical method.
text.formatted: In traditional, methodological simulation studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Morris et al., 2019)</ref>, the targets of interest are usually the unknown parameters of the data-generating mechanism, which are estimated with a statistical method.

text.text: In contrast, the targets in LLM simulation studies are quantitative or qualitative characteristics of the text stimuli in terms of the psychological variables of interest.
Correspondingly, the estimands of LLM-generated ratings are the unknown (numeric or discrete) values of the items on the variables to be rated.
This section provides information about the different models and prompt variants that will be analyzed in the LLM simulation (cf.
Figure 1).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: The chosen method factors should be accompanied with a clear description and justification to ensure that readers can judge the scope of the LLM simulation (i.e., which range of model specifications has been investigated).
The combination of all method factors varied in the LLM simulation determines the simulation design and the number of simulation conditions.
It should be stated which LLMs will be used.

LLMs differ in numerous aspects such as the architecture (often referred to as model family), the number of parameters (i.e., model size), the company or institution developing a model, the languages in which an LLM was trained, and whether information about the model weights and training procedure is publicly available.
If possible, justify why the employed models were selected.

The reasoning for choosing specific models may concern availability, expected costs, openness, and/or computational feasibility (e.g., maximum model size that can be run locally). 2A fully factorial design encompassing all combinations of LLM families and model sizes is often infeasible, as not all models are available across different size variants.
text.formatted: The reasoning for choosing specific models may concern availability, expected costs, openness, and/or computational feasibility (e.g., maximum model size that can be run locally). <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">2</ref>A fully factorial design encompassing all combinations of LLM families and model sizes is often infeasible, as not all models are available across different size variants.

text.text: Thus, we recommend including all investigated LLM variants as a single factor in the analysis as opposed to handling certain aspects (e.g., model family and model size) as separate factors.

Furthermore, report the values of all model hyperparameters that may affect the output (e.g., temperature, top-p, top-k, context length, seed, batch size), including those that were not changed from their defaults.
Default values may change between software versions, differ between models, and be overridden by the software used to access a model.

For instance, in our case study, the documented default temperature of 0.8 in Ollama was replaced by a value of 1 because the models were accessed through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (see Appendix B).
This shows that it can be necessary to verify the effective settings rather than relying on the documentation.
If hyperparameters are adjusted for each model, it is appropriate to treat all LLM variants as a single factor.

Otherwise, if systematic variations of LLM settings (e.g., temperature, which controls the degree of stochasticity of the output) are of interest, these hyperparameters can be treated as separate method factors.
For example, one may manipulate temperature and top-p in a factorial grid to study their relative impact on the variability and quality of LLM ratings.
The Methods section also describes the different prompt versions provided to the LLMs.

Specify all components of the prompt input that vary across simulation conditions, such as different system prompts that may contain context about the purpose of the task, instructions for the LLM on which scale to return ratings, and whether examples are provided or not (zero-shot vs. few-shot prompting; Feuerriegel et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Specify all components of the prompt input that vary across simulation conditions, such as different system prompts that may contain context about the purpose of the task, instructions for the LLM on which scale to return ratings, and whether examples are provided or not (zero-shot vs. few-shot prompting; <ref type="bibr">Feuerriegel et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these prompt components defines a method factor.
In a fully factorial design, distinct prompt versions are obtained by combining all levels of the different prompt components.
If some of the combinations do not result in meaningful prompt instructions, one may use an incomplete factorial design or treat the subset of meaningful combinations as a single factor.
To ensure that the comparison of LLM rating quality across models is valid, the same prompt versions should be used for all LLM versions.
The Performance Measures section provides information on how the consistency and agreement of LLM ratings will be evaluated and how the uncertainty of this evaluation will be quantified.
The section also concerns the handling of missing values and the interpretation of performance measures, as well as the number of iterations in each simulation condition.
To avoid ambiguity, one may also specify equations for how these measures will be calculated.
The choice of specific performance measures depends on the aims of the investigation.

If the aim is to analyze the consistency in terms of the proportion of variance in LLM ratings due to different LLM model versions or prompt instructions, it is necessary to specify a suitable mixed-effects model for variance decomposition of the LLM simulation design.
Generalizability theory provides a natural framework for such an analysis, which proceeds in two steps (Brennan, 2001).
text.formatted: Generalizability theory provides a natural framework for such an analysis, which proceeds in two steps <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brennan, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: In the G study, a mixed model is used to estimate the variance components of the object of measurement (typically the stimuli), of all facets (e.g., model, prompt components), and of their interactions.
In the D study, these components are combined into reliability coefficients for a specific measurement design, that is, for ratings averaged across a given number of conditions per facet.

The generalizability coefficient Eρ 2 quantifies how consistently the relative ordering of the stimuli is reproduced across facet conditions, whereas the dependability coefficient Φ additionally takes differences in the absolute level of the ratings into account.

Because a D study can be computed for any number of conditions per facet, researchers can also project how reliability will change if different numbers of models, prompt variants, or iterations are used.

When planning the analysis, researchers should specify the mixed model, which facets are treated as random or fixed, how the universe score is defined, which coefficient is of primary interest, and which D study designs will be evaluated.
The case study below illustrates these steps in detail.
Importantly, high consistency across simulation conditions does not imply that the output is correct or valid.
High estimates of consistency can also emerge if LLMs systematically give incorrect or biased responses.
Therefore, the weak validation criterion is not sufficient by itself to judge the quality of LLM ratings.
Still, the approach is useful as a first step to identify methodological factors that shape LLM response distributions when an external criterion is not (yet) available.

If an external criterion is available for comparison (e.g., human ratings), the inter-rater reliability between human ratings and LLM ratings may be computed as the Pearson or rank-order correlation of ratings across all stimulus materials (Goodwin, 2001).
text.formatted: If an external criterion is available for comparison (e.g., human ratings), the inter-rater reliability between human ratings and LLM ratings may be computed as the Pearson or rank-order correlation of ratings across all stimulus materials <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Goodwin, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The choice between measures of relative and absolute agreement should follow from the intended use of the LLM ratings.

The distinction between relative and absolute agreement parallels the generalizability and dependability coefficients in generalizability theory, which concern the relative ordering and the absolute level of ratings, respectively (Brennan, 2001).
text.formatted: The distinction between relative and absolute agreement parallels the generalizability and dependability coefficients in generalizability theory, which concern the relative ordering and the absolute level of ratings, respectively <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brennan, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Measures of relative agreement (e.g., Pearson or rank-order correlations, or the consistency intraclass correlation ICC(C,1); McGraw and Wong, 1996) are sufficient when LLM ratings are used to order stimuli, to select stimuli covering the range of a construct, or as covariates or predictors in statistical models, since these uses are unaffected by linear transformations of the ratings.

Measures of absolute agreement (e.g., mean bias, root mean square error across items, or the agreement intraclass correlation ICC(A,1)) are required whenever the generated values themselves are interpreted, for instance, when LLM ratings are combined with existing human norms, when stimuli are selected based on cutoff values (e.g., to select "neutral" items), or when LLMs are used to predict or forecast observable quantities such as voting behavior (von der Heyde et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Measures of absolute agreement (e.g., mean bias, root mean square error across items, or the agreement intraclass correlation ICC(A,1)) are required whenever the generated values themselves are interpreted, for instance, when LLM ratings are combined with existing human norms, when stimuli are selected based on cutoff values (e.g., to select "neutral" items), or when LLMs are used to predict or forecast observable quantities such as voting behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(von der Heyde et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Because high correlations do not preclude systematic shifts or a compressed range of LLM ratings (Abdurahman et al., 2024), researchers may additionally compare the distributions of LLM and human ratings (e.g., means and standard deviations).
text.formatted: Because high correlations do not preclude systematic shifts or a compressed range of LLM ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abdurahman et al., 2024)</ref>, researchers may additionally compare the distributions of LLM and human ratings (e.g., means and standard deviations).

text.text: For any measure, one should specify whether LLM ratings are averaged across prompt iterations before computing the mean across items.

Furthermore, researchers may employ a rater non-inferiority criterion, demanding that the agreement between LLM and human ratings should be as high as the agreement between different human raters (Cummins et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Furthermore, researchers may employ a rater non-inferiority criterion, demanding that the agreement between LLM and human ratings should be as high as the agreement between different human raters <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Cummins et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: If a study targets specific comparisons between LLM configurations (e.g., whether a smaller local model agrees with human ratings as well as a commercial model), these comparisons can be tested statistically.
Because both correlations share the same benchmark ratings, they are dependent, and tests for independent correlations are not appropriate.
Suitable tests and confidence intervals for dependent correlations are implemented, for instance, in the R package cocor (Diedenhofen & Musch, 2015).
text.formatted: Suitable tests and confidence intervals for dependent correlations are implemented, for instance, in the R package cocor <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Diedenhofen & Musch, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Such targeted tests are most informative when the comparisons are specified in advance; in exploratory multiverse designs, the number of possible pairwise comparisons grows quickly, so that summarizing the overall pattern (e.g., by variance components or plots of all conditions) is often more useful than testing every pair.

Researchers may be interested in computing logprobs of token predictions to obtain probability-weighted expected ratings that reflect the uncertainty associated with each token (e.g., Hussain et al., 2024; Martínez et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Researchers may be interested in computing logprobs of token predictions to obtain probability-weighted expected ratings that reflect the uncertainty associated with each token (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Hussain et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The estimation uncertainty of some performance measures (such as the correlation of LLM and human ratings) is bounded by the number n items of stimulus items included in the study.
The sampling error due to having a finite number of items is relevant with respect to generalizing the results to other items from the target domain (Brennan, 2010).
text.formatted: The sampling error due to having a finite number of items is relevant with respect to generalizing the results to other items from the target domain <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Brennan, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: To assess this type of uncertainty, we can average the standard error of an agreement measure across simulation iterations (e.g., the mean SE of the correlation coefficient).
Importantly, the averaged standard error depends on the number of items and does not automatically decrease even if more conditions or iterations are used.
A different source of uncertainty in LLM simulations is due to the stochasticity of repeated LLM ratings within the same condition (Knöchel et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A different source of uncertainty in LLM simulations is due to the stochasticity of repeated LLM ratings within the same condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Knöchel et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This uncertainty can be reported in the form of the Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) and decreases for a larger number of iterations.

When studying the quality of LLM-generated ratings, we consider the MCSE to be less relevant than the uncertainty due to studying only a limited number of items, since it depends on a property of the specific procedure (i.e., how many repeated LLM ratings were elicited) and not a property of the content (i.e., whether the rating methodology generalized across the item domain).
LLM output can deviate from the allowed range of responses, resulting in invalid or missing values.

If ratings are to be confined to numerical values in a bounded, predefined range (e.g., Likert ratings between 1 and 7), provide information on how other output (e.g., non-numeric text or values outside of the range) will be treated.
One possibility is to handle these values as missing data and report their relative occurrence rate.

To reduce such issues, researchers can use LLM software that ensures a certain output structure, for instance, by specifying a specific JSON template (for example with software packages such as ellmer in R; Wickham et al., 2025).
text.formatted: To reduce such issues, researchers can use LLM software that ensures a certain output structure, for instance, by specifying a specific JSON template (for example with software packages such as ellmer in R; <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Wickham et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: If such methods are not used, it may be the case that the rating of interest is still included in the open text output and can potentially be retrieved by further text processing.
If this is the case, describe the steps taken to extract relevant information from the open text format.

As an alternative to treating invalid responses as missings, it is possible to impute iterations that did not return a valid rating, for instance, by implementing repeated prompting until a valid output rating is obtained (for different strategies of handling missingness in simulations, see Pawel et al., 2026).
text.formatted: As an alternative to treating invalid responses as missings, it is possible to impute iterations that did not return a valid rating, for instance, by implementing repeated prompting until a valid output rating is obtained (for different strategies of handling missingness in simulations, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Pawel et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, specify at which proportion of failed iterations a whole condition will be excluded from the analysis.
Finally, one may specify thresholds to reduce post-hoc flexibility in interpreting the results.
For example, one could specify what will constitute 'acceptable' and 'unacceptable' levels of performance and what will count as 'relevant differences' in the performance of different LLMs.
Still, any verbal labels should be interpreted cautiously, especially if they are based on arbitrary conventions.
The last section of the template documents the employed software versions and the computational environment used for the LLM simulation.
List the primary packages intended for LLM usage, including their version number.
Additionally, include information about the operating system that will be used for running all analyses and for hosting the LLMs.
If different computers or servers are utilized for the LLM simulation and the subsequent analysis, report information regarding each of these environments.
After the analysis, the code employed to execute all analyses, as well as the intermediate or complete results of the analyses should be stored in an open online repository.
Supplemental materials may also be provided to ensure a comprehensive documentation of the employed methodology (Argyle et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Supplemental materials may also be provided to ensure a comprehensive documentation of the employed methodology <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Argyle et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This section can also include information about the most likely obstacles in LLM prompting (e.g., issues with the API or LLM service due to repeated requests) or the simulation design, and plans to overcome them.

As a case study, we present a preregistered application of the modified ADEMP and 5 validated GPT-4o ratings of valence and arousal, respectively, against human ratings for two different sets of 96 multi-word expressions, yielding correlations of r = .95 (valence) and r = .92 (arousal).
We conducted two separate LLM simulation studies-one for valence and one for arousal-since ratings for the two constructs were validated using different item sets.
In each simulation, we varied the choice of LLM and the prompt structure by manipulating the required response format and the type of prompt examples provided as context.

Assessing both consistency and inter-rater reliability, our analyses focused on the variance decomposition of LLM-generated ratings and the correlation of LLM and human ratings of valence and arousal provided by Martínez et al. (2024).
text.formatted: Assessing both consistency and inter-rater reliability, our analyses focused on the variance decomposition of LLM-generated ratings and the correlation of LLM and human ratings of valence and arousal provided by <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: Before conducting the reported simulation study, we ran preliminary tests to assess the usefulness of the modified ADEMP template and ascertain the functionality of the analysis pipeline.
For this purpose, we evaluated the quality of LLM ratings regarding the syntactic complexity of factual statements using the items and human ratings by Schmidt and Heck (2024).
text.formatted: For this purpose, we evaluated the quality of LLM ratings regarding the syntactic complexity of factual statements using the items and human ratings by <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Schmidt and Heck (2024)</ref>.

text.text: We used the ADEMP template for LLM simulation studies for planning and preregistration (https://osf.io/8e6gf). 3 We report the results for valence in the main text and those for arousal in the supplementary materials (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23810473).
text.formatted: We used the ADEMP template for LLM simulation studies for planning and preregistration (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/8e6gf">https://osf.io/8e6gf</ref>). <ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">3</ref> We report the results for valence in the main text and those for arousal in the supplementary materials (<ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23810473">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23810473</ref>).

text.text: The aims of the LLM simulation study are (1) to conduct a variance decomposition of LLM ratings of valence and arousal regarding multi-word expressions into construct variance (due to differences in the valence and arousal of the included items) and method variance (due to specific LLM and prompt variations) and ( 2) to assess the extent to which LLM ratings correspond to the perceived valence and arousal of multi-word expressions as rated by humans.
text.formatted: The aims of the LLM simulation study are (1) to conduct a variance decomposition of LLM ratings of valence and arousal regarding multi-word expressions into construct variance (due to differences in the valence and arousal of the included items) and method variance (due to specific LLM and prompt variations) and ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_1">2</ref>) to assess the extent to which LLM ratings correspond to the perceived valence and arousal of multi-word expressions as rated by humans.

text.text: Our study uses two different sets of English multi-word expressions (each with n items = 96 items). Martínez et al. (2024) selected the stimuli based on their own GPT-4o ratings to cover the entire range of the respective construct.
text.formatted: Our study uses two different sets of English multi-word expressions (each with n items = 96 items). <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al. (2024)</ref> selected the stimuli based on their own GPT-4o ratings to cover the entire range of the respective construct.

text.text: In Experiments 4 and 5, human raters rated the stimuli regarding valence and arousal, respectively.
All analyses were conducted separately for the multi-word expressions of valence and arousal but with identical methodology reported in the Methods section.
All LLM calls were independent by starting each LLM call with a fresh context (also see Conde et al., 2026).
text.formatted: All LLM calls were independent by starting each LLM call with a fresh context (also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Conde et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: We used open-weights LLMs which are run locally through the software Ollama (Ollama, 2026) and are accessed via the R package ellmer.
text.formatted: We used open-weights LLMs which are run locally through the software Ollama <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Ollama, 2026)</ref> and are accessed via the R package ellmer.

text.text: To ensure that LLM ratings of valence and arousal only consist of numerical values, we used the type_object() and type_integer() functions to request output in JSON format with a predetermined response format of integers.
Each prompt is composed according to the structure used by Martínez et al. (2024) in prompt 2 (valence) and prompt 3 (arousal) of their paper: (1)

text.text: An explanation of the task, (2) the range of responses allowed, (3) examples for multi-word expressions, (4) the target multi-word expression to be rated, and (5) a reminder for the range of responses allowed.
Our target estimands are the valence and arousal of multi-word expressions (where the scale varies across conditions as detailed in the Methods section in the following).
Valence and arousal are the two primary variables of dimensional models of affect (Russell, 1980).
text.formatted: Valence and arousal are the two primary variables of dimensional models of affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Russell, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Valence refers to the pleasantness of a stimulus, ranging from very negative to very positive, whereas arousal refers to the intensity of the emotional activation elicited by a stimulus, ranging from calm to excited (Warriner et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Valence refers to the pleasantness of a stimulus, ranging from very negative to very positive, whereas arousal refers to the intensity of the emotional activation elicited by a stimulus, ranging from calm to excited <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Warriner et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: We included eight open-weights models by four companies that can efficiently be run locally using
Ollama on a GPU with 32GB VRAM without requiring access to an online service.

The eight models were gemma3 (with 4b, 12b, and 27b parameters; Google)foot_3 , llama3.1 (8b parameters; Meta), phi3 (3.8b, 14b parameters; Microsoft), phi4 (14b parameters; Microsoft), and gpt-oss (20b parameters; OpenAI).
text.formatted: The eight models were gemma3 (with 4b, 12b, and 27b parameters; Google)<ref type="foot" target="#foot_3">foot_3</ref> , llama3.1 (8b parameters; Meta), phi3 (3.8b, 14b parameters; Microsoft), phi4 (14b parameters; Microsoft), and gpt-oss (20b parameters; OpenAI).

text.text: All model parameters were kept at the values that applied by default in our software setup.

We deliberately did not tune these settings, because default configurations correspond to how most researchers will use these models in practice, which makes the results informative for typical applications.

Although Ollama documents a default temperature of 0.8 for models without a model-specific value (llama3.1:8b, phi3:3.8b, phi3:14b, phi4:14b), accessing Ollama via ellmer sets temperature and top-p to 1 for all requests.
Hence, all eight models ran with the same temperature and top-p, whereas top-k was 64 for the gemma3 models and 40 for all other models.

Appendix B documents all settings, and an additional check in the supplementary materials confirmed empirically that ratings obtained with the default settings corresponded to those obtained with a temperature of 1 rather than 0.8.
All models were updated to their most recent version at 28/01/2026.

We adopted the prompt design by Martínez et al. (2024) to obtain either a valence or an arousal rating while manipulating two key components in a fully factorial setting: (1) The format of the rating task (a 1-9 or a 0-100 scale) and ( 2) The presence and type of example expressions provided: no example expressions; three examples for low valence or arousal (lower anchor); three examples for high valence or arousal (upper anchor); or three examples for both low and high valence or arousal (both lower and upper anchor).

(2024)</ref> to obtain either a valence or an arousal rating while manipulating two key components in a fully factorial setting: (1) The format of the rating task (a 1-9 or a 0-100 scale) and ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_1">2</ref>) The presence and type of example expressions provided: no example expressions; three examples for low valence or arousal (lower anchor); three examples for high valence or arousal (upper anchor); or three examples for both low and high valence or arousal (both lower and upper anchor).

text.text: The last condition corresponds to the original prompt design used by Martínez et al. (2024).
text.formatted: The last condition corresponds to the original prompt design used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: Ratings of valence and arousal were obtained in two separate and independent steps of the LLM simulation.
The system prompt was empty, thus not providing any custom system instructions.
Example prompts can be found in the Appendix.

The complete LLM simulation design including all investigated method factors had 8 × 2 ×4 = 64 distinct conditions in total, as summarized by the following list: • Model: eight models from four different companies, run locally using Ollama • Format: response scale, ranging either from 1 to 9 or from 0 to 100, that the LLMs had to adhere to in their response • Example: four types of different examples provided to the LLMs (none, lower anchor, upper anchor, both lower and upper anchor)

The present investigation used two performance measures: (1) Estimating the variance components in LLM-generated valence and arousal ratings associated with differences in the stimulus materials and differences in methods (secondary performance measure focusing on consistency), and (2) assessing the correlation between human and LLM ratings of valence and arousal (primary performance measure focusing on inter-rater reliability).

Regarding aim (1), we estimated the variance components of the following linear mixed model using the gtheory package (Moore, 2016) which uses the lmer() function, lmer(llm_rating ~(1 | stimulus * model * format * example),...
text.formatted: Regarding aim (1), we estimated the variance components of the following linear mixed model using the gtheory package <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Moore, 2016)</ref> which uses the lmer() function, lmer(llm_rating ~(1 | stimulus * model * format * example),...

text.text: The stimulus term accounts for differences in the target construct between the multi-word expressions (i.e., actual variability in valence or arousal), whereas the remaining terms (model, format, and example) account for methods effects.

Following generalizability theory, we first performed a G study, in which the variance components of all random effects (main effects and interactions) were estimated from the fitted model and expressed as percentages of their sum (Brennan, 2001).
text.formatted: Following generalizability theory, we first performed a G study, in which the variance components of all random effects (main effects and interactions) were estimated from the fitted model and expressed as percentages of their sum <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brennan, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: All variance components were estimated as random effects because each model, example type, and response format is drawn from a potentially infinite universe with the stimuli being the object of measurement.
The realization of the chosen model, exact example type, and presentation of the response format are to some extent arbitrary and interchangeable and could differ across studies.
Treating any of these facets as fixed would move interactions of the stimuli with these facets to the universe score variance and thereby increase the generalizability and dependability coefficients.
The present analysis can therefore be regarded as conservative.

In the D study, the universe score of a stimulus is its expected rating across all admissible conditions of the facets (e.g., across all models and prompt variants that could have been used), and the variance of these scores across stimuli constitutes the universe score variance.

We defined it as σ 2 (τ ) = σ 2 (stimulus) (i.e., as the true, unknown random-intercept variance of the stimuli), because we aimed to evaluate how well the obtained stimulus LLM ratings generalize across the investigated facets of the design (8 models, 4 example conditions, 2 response formats).

The generalizability coefficient compares the universe score variance to the relative error variance σ 2 (δ), which comprises all components involving an interaction with the stimuli and thus affects the relative ordering of stimulus ratings.
In contrast, the dependability coefficient is based on the absolute error variance σ 2 (∆), which additionally includes facet main effects and their interactions, so that Φ ≤ Eρ 2 .

Our analysis focuses on Eρ 2 , as our study focuses on whether LLMs can produce stimulus ratings that show the same relative ordering (but not necessarily the exact same values) as those provided by humans.

The D study variance components were obtained by dividing the respective G study variance components by the product of the number of factor levels per involved facet (excluding the object of measurement -the stimuli).

For example, the D study variance component for the interaction of the stimulus s, the model facet m, and the example facet e is given by σ 2 (sM E) = σ 2 (sme) , where σ 2 (sme) is the corresponding G study variance component and n ′ m and n ′ e are the number of models (= 8) and example conditions (= 4), respectively.
The capital letters M and E indicate that the estimated variance component is for stimulus mean scores across 8 models and 4 example type conditions.
Because σ 2 (sM E) involves an interaction with the stimuli, it is part of σ 2 (δ), whereas components without such an interaction (e.g., σ 2 (M E)) enter only the absolute error variance σ 2 (∆).
