We computed the correlation at two different levels of the analysis: • (a) At the level of individual iterations in each simulation condition, we computed the correlation between human ratings and LLM ratings across expressions.
The inter-rater reliability (IRR) was estimated by the average correlation,

To assess the estimation error due to the finite number of iterations, we computed the Monte Carlo standard error, where is the sample standard deviation of the estimate and n sim is the number of simulation iterations (see Siepe et al., 2024).

text.text: • (b) At the level of aggregated LLM ratings (averaged across all simulation iterations within each simulation condition), we computed the correlation between human and LLM ratings.

Using a bootstrap procedure, n est LLM ratings were first randomly drawn with replacement from the n sim iterations of a simulation condition for each stimulus and then aggregated into an average rating.
These average ratings per stimulus were then used to compute the inter-rater reliability between human-generated and LLM-generated ratings.
This procedure was repeated n sim times to ensure that the same number of estimates was obtained as when using raw LLM ratings.

Regarding our primary performance measure, the correlation between human and LLM ratings, we preregistered the following thresholds: an inter-rater reliability of IRR ≥ .70 was labeled acceptable, IRR ≥ .80 adequate, and IRR ≥ .90 (as obtained with GPT-4o by Martínez et al., 2024) excellent.

text.text: The specific cutoffs and their verbal labels should therefore not be read as substantive quality categories, but rather serve to constrain post-hoc flexibility in interpreting the results.
The continuous estimates and their uncertainty remain the primary basis for interpretation.
We considered a certain method as performing better (or worse) than these thresholds on the employed corpus if the MCSE 95% CI was above (below) a threshold.

We considered Method X as performing better than Method Y in a certain simulation condition on the employed corpus if the lower bound for the estimated inter-rater reliability of Method X ( IRR -1.96 • MCSE) was greater than the upper bound for the estimated inter-rater reliability of Method Y ( IRR + 1.96 • MCSE).

Conversely, if the 95% CI based on the averaged standard errors of correlation coefficients between human-generated and LLM-generated ratings was above (below) one of the thresholds, we concluded that a certain method is generally better (worse) than this threshold for comparable stimulus material.
As noted above, the MCSE-based CI only reflects the precision of the estimate in a condition, not whether performance generalizes to new stimuli.

text.text: To assess whether the performance ranking of LLM simulation conditions generalizes to new stimuli, we conducted a split-half analysis (exploratory).
We randomly split the 96 stimuli into two halves of 48 stimuli each.

Within each half, we computed the correlation between human and LLM ratings for each condition and iteration and averaged these correlations across iterations, yielding 64 average correlations per half (one per condition).
We then computed the Pearson and Spearman correlations between the two halves across the 64 conditions.

Repeating this procedure for 1,000 random splits yielded a mean split-half correlation of r = .95 [.90, .98] and a mean rank correlation of r s = .90 [.83, .95] (values within square brackets indicate 95% percentiles).
Applying the Spearman-Brown formula to estimate the stability for the full set of 96 stimuli yielded r = .97 and r s = .95.
Thus, the relative performance of the LLM simulation conditions was highly stable across independent sets of stimuli.
However, this stability does not guarantee that the findings generalize to new datasets (see next section).

The present work proposes a systematic workflow for evaluating the quality of LLM-generated ratings for stimulus materials.
We take a novel perspective by connecting LLM-based methodology for natural language processing with traditional methodological simulation studies.

Our framework enhances the coherence across disparate fields that have used LLMs to elicit ratings and promotes the adoption of rigorous methodological standards that have been effective in related disciplines.

To this end, we adapted the ADEMP framework originally proposed in the field of statistics for simulation studies (Morris et al., 2019) and the corresponding ADEMP-PreReg template (Siepe et al., 2024).

text.text: Besides rigorous method evaluation, the multiverse approach can also be useful for exploring the impact of different methodological factors, such as model type, hyperparameter settings, or prompt details.
Once a strong configuration has been identified for a given task, subsequent evaluations can compare new models or prompting strategies against this best-performing configuration.

Due to the fully crossed design of a multiverse study, its computational costs are much higher than those of a single LLM setup, especially for large stimulus sets such as the norms of concreteness, valence, and arousal generated by Martínez et al. (2024) for 126,397 single words and 63,680 multi-word expressions.

(2024)</ref> for 126,397 single words and 63,680 multi-word expressions.

text.text: These costs can be limited by applying an ADEMP validation study to a random subset of stimuli from the target corpus.
Because the subset is a random sample, the findings generalize to the remaining stimuli, with the item-based standard error quantifying the uncertainty of this generalization.
The best-performing configuration can then be used to rate the full corpus, for which obtaining human ratings would be infeasible (e.g., Beucler et al., 2026; Martínez et al., 2024).

text.text: However, stimulus sets that cover all areas of the response distribution equally, as in the present case study, may increase construct (universe score) variance and thereby lead to an overestimation of the generalizability coefficient.
We illustrated the new ADEMP template by conceptually replicating and extending the validation study by Martínez et al. (2024).
text.formatted: We illustrated the new ADEMP template by conceptually replicating and extending the validation study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: In line with their findings, we observed high correlations between human and LLM ratings of valence and arousal.

However, with smaller local models, rating quality depended on the chosen model and, to a lesser extent, on the response format and prompt examples, particularly in combination, as quantified by the variance components (Brennan, 2001).
text.formatted: However, with smaller local models, rating quality depended on the chosen model and, to a lesser extent, on the response format and prompt examples, particularly in combination, as quantified by the variance components <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brennan, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: A limitation is that subjective human ratings served as the benchmark, which need not be correct and can be distorted by inattentive responding and other response biases (e.g., Stosic et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A limitation is that subjective human ratings served as the benchmark, which need not be correct and can be distorted by inattentive responding and other response biases (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Stosic et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Given the high reliability of the human ratings and the difficulty of measuring valence and arousal otherwise, however, there seems to be no better alternative benchmark.

Despite the sensitivity of LLM-generated ratings to methodological choices, even modestly sized, locally run open-weight models with approximately 8 to 27 billion parameters produced valence ratings that correlated with human ratings comparably to GPT-4o, particularly when ratings were averaged over repeated queries under identical conditions.
Concerning limitations, LLM performance may vary even for related constructs:
For arousal, open-weight models reached only adequate performance (r ≈ .80; see Results), below that of GPT-4o (Martínez et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For arousal, open-weight models reached only adequate performance (r ≈ .80; see Results), below that of GPT-4o <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Martínez et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This may partly reflect properties of the construct, since arousal ratings are generally less consistent across norming studies than valence ratings (Muraki & Pexman, 2025; Warriner et al., 2013).
text.formatted: This may partly reflect properties of the construct, since arousal ratings are generally less consistent across norming studies than valence ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Muraki & Pexman, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Warriner et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, the paper and data by Martínez et al. (2024) may have been part of the training data of some models (e.g., gpt-oss and gemma3, published in 2025), which could inflate performance estimates ("leakage"; Feuerriegel et al., 2025; Hullman et al., 2026), possibly more so for valence than for arousal.
text.formatted: Alternatively, the paper and data by <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al. (2024)</ref> may have been part of the training data of some models (e.g., gpt-oss and gemma3, published in 2025), which could inflate performance estimates ("leakage"; <ref type="bibr">Feuerriegel et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Hullman et al., 2026)</ref>, possibly more so for valence than for arousal.

text.text: Ruling out this explanation requires replicating the present investigation with new stimulus materials and human ratings.

Finally, other procedural details besides model type, prompt examples, and response scale may affect LLM response quality; while we selected those deemed most relevant, future research is required to study other prompt design choices (Fang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Finally, other procedural details besides model type, prompt examples, and response scale may affect LLM response quality; while we selected those deemed most relevant, future research is required to study other prompt design choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Fang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A fundamental caveat concerns the interpretation of LLMs' predictive performance.

While LLM output may show high correlations of up to .95 with human ratings, such high predictive performance does not imply that LLMs have a causal understanding of cognitive processes in humans or that the underlying mechanisms are equivalent (Demszky et al., 2023). Loru et al. (2025) investigated this question and showed that LLMs produced output similar to that of human raters in a news classification task, but humans and LLMs still differed in the processes leading to their conclusions.
text.formatted: While LLM output may show high correlations of up to .95 with human ratings, such high predictive performance does not imply that LLMs have a causal understanding of cognitive processes in humans or that the underlying mechanisms are equivalent <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Demszky et al., 2023)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Loru et al. (2025)</ref> investigated this question and showed that LLMs produced output similar to that of human raters in a news classification task, but humans and LLMs still differed in the processes leading to their conclusions.

text.text: Furthermore, high correlations between LLM and human ratings do not justify simply replacing human participants with LLMs.

Rather, systematic LLM simulations varying procedural details, planned and possibly preregistered with the ADEMP template, allow researchers to investigate where discrepancies between LLM and human ratings may occur and which factors are relevant for minimizing this gap.
When using commercial LLMs as a research tool, the lack of information about model architecture as well as training data and procedures threatens scientific transparency and reproducibility.
Additionally, many large models cannot be run locally and are accessible exclusively through APIs (Feuerriegel et al., 2025; Wulff & Mata, 2025a).
text.formatted: Additionally, many large models cannot be run locally and are accessible exclusively through APIs <ref type="bibr">(Feuerriegel et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Wulff & Mata, 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, we employed open-weight models run locally using Ollama (Ollama, 2026), accessed via ellmer in R (Wickham et al., 2025), thereby enabling other researchers to easily replicate and extend our analyses.
text.formatted: In the present study, we employed open-weight models run locally using Ollama <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Ollama, 2026)</ref>, accessed via ellmer in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Wickham et al., 2025)</ref>, thereby enabling other researchers to easily replicate and extend our analyses.

text.text: When accessed via programming languages such as Python, open models even allow researchers to access internal model information such as log probabilities of LLM predictions (which reflect the uncertainty associated with each response) or to apply fine-tuning to further increase the correlation with human ratings (Hussain et al., 2024; Martínez et al., 2024).
text.formatted: When accessed via programming languages such as Python, open models even allow researchers to access internal model information such as log probabilities of LLM predictions (which reflect the uncertainty associated with each response) or to apply fine-tuning to further increase the correlation with human ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Hussain et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, open-weights models are not without limitations.
For instance, even if the architecture and weights are openly available, the complete set of factors, design choices, and training data relevant to their development may not be known.

Another general issue is the substantial computational and environmental cost of LLMs (Abdurahman et al., 2024; Debelak et al., 2025; Demszky et al., 2023), which can be mitigated by smaller models that run locally on consumer-level hardware.
text.formatted: Another general issue is the substantial computational and environmental cost of LLMs <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abdurahman et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Debelak et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Demszky et al., 2023)</ref>, which can be mitigated by smaller models that run locally on consumer-level hardware.

text.text: Costs also increase with the context length (i.e., the number of input and output words a model can consider; Hussain et al., 2024), and long inputs may be more difficult for LLMs to process (Huang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Costs also increase with the context length (i.e., the number of input and output words a model can consider; <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Hussain et al., 2024)</ref>, and long inputs may be more difficult for LLMs to process <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Huang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the present investigation, we used concise rating instructions and requested only integer ratings, thus keeping context length minimal.
Finally, LLM output may be biased related to demographic factors such as race or sex.

This is especially critical when using LLMs for rating tasks, as LLMs may replicate existing societal biases present in their training data (Abdurahman et al., 2025; Debelak et al., 2025; Guest et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This is especially critical when using LLMs for rating tasks, as LLMs may replicate existing societal biases present in their training data <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abdurahman et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Debelak et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Guest et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: By conducting an LLM simulation study using the present framework, researchers can investigate biases.

On the one hand, biases not specific to particular items will manifest as changes in the absolute level of all LLM ratings, and thus in a larger main effect of model type on stimulus ratings (e.g., generally higher ratings for one model than another model).

On the other hand, model biases specific to certain item properties will manifest as an interaction between model and stimulus type (e.g., systematically different ratings for items involving men vs. women). 8For instance, researchers may systematically vary certain terms and content related to specific demographic groups in the stimulus materials (e.g., whether an applicant is framed as male or female) to examine how specific aspects affect LLM ratings.
text.formatted: On the other hand, model biases specific to certain item properties will manifest as an interaction between model and stimulus type (e.g., systematically different ratings for items involving men vs. women). <ref type="foot" target="#foot_6">8</ref>For instance, researchers may systematically vary certain terms and content related to specific demographic groups in the stimulus materials (e.g., whether an applicant is framed as male or female) to examine how specific aspects affect LLM ratings.

text.text: The proposed template can also be used for more specialized and advanced methods of eliciting LLM ratings.
For instance, researchers may forgo LLM prompting altogether and instead extract psychological constructs from text data using embedding spaces provided by certain models.

Recent studies have used embedding spaces to analyze semantic relationships between various psychological constructs and item texts (e.g., Herderich et al., 2024; Hommel and Arslan, 2025; Hommel et al., 2026; Wulff and Mata, 2025b).
text.formatted: Recent studies have used embedding spaces to analyze semantic relationships between various psychological constructs and item texts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Herderich et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Hommel and Arslan, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Hommel et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Wulff and Mata, 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, fine-tuning can tailor LLMs to specific tasks (Conde et al., 2026; Hussain et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Similarly, fine-tuning can tailor LLMs to specific tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Conde et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Hussain et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although a multiverse of design choices is not strictly needed for continually improving a fine-tuned model, the ADEMP approach can help evaluate how the choice of base model and hyperparameter settings affects the resulting fine-tuned models.
In conclusion, the present paper contributes to the robust use of language models as a research tool by developing a workflow for evaluating LLM-generated ratings.
We adapted the ADEMP template for statistical simulation studies to facilitate the planning and reporting of LLM simulations.

The framework draws on generalizability theory to disentangle the contributions of items, model and prompt choices as well as repeated iterations to the consistency of LLM ratings (Brennan, 2001; Cronbach, 1972), while using inter-rater reliability with human ratings as a gold standard for validity (Goodwin, 2001).
text.formatted: The framework draws on generalizability theory to disentangle the contributions of items, model and prompt choices as well as repeated iterations to the consistency of LLM ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brennan, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Cronbach, 1972)</ref>, while using inter-rater reliability with human ratings as a gold standard for validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Goodwin, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, our framework provides a psychometric perspective on evaluating LLM output across the multiverse of arbitrary model and prompt choices.

All LLM calls were run successively on a single GPU (RTX 5090, 32 GB VRAM).

text.text: Consequently, the parameters in effect in our simulation were: • temperature = 1 and top-p = 1 for all models • top-k = 64 for gemma3 (4b, 12b, 27b) and top-k = 40 for all other models • num_ctx = 8192 for gpt-oss (20b) and num_ctx = 4096 for all other models • all remaining parameters at the Ollama or Modelfile defaults listed above

The supplementary temperature analysis (20 iterations per condition with default settings and temperatures of 0.8 and 1.0) is consistent with these settings; ratings obtained with default settings corresponded to those obtained with a temperature of 1 rather than 0.8.
Note that the documentation of ellmer 0.4.0 states that models accessed via Ollama "can only use 2048 input tokens".
This note does not reflect the effective context length in our setup (see above).
All prompts in our simulation were far shorter than 2048 tokens, so that none of the context limits affected the input.
The gpt-oss override further illustrates that effective settings can deviate from documented defaults and should be verified in the source code or empirically.
